opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think the "sudden" part is a bit of an illusion. A lot of things had to be in place first, and once they were, it looked like an overnight success.

The biggest piece is that the base models got good enough. RL is really about amplifying behaviors the model can already produce some of the time. If your pretrained model almost never stumbles onto a correct chain of reasoning for a hard math problem, there's no signal to reinforce. You're sampling in the dark. But once pretraining at scale gave us models that could sometimes get it right, sometimes backtrack, sometimes catch their own mistakes, then a simple reward like "did you get the right answer" becomes extremely informative. You're selecting for the reasoning strategies that actually work, and the model learns to use them more reliably and for longer.

The second piece is the verifiable reward itself. People tried RL from human preferences for a long time, and it's useful, but learned reward models can be hacked. The policy finds quirks in the reward model and exploits them. With math answers that can be checked, or code that has to pass unit tests, the reward is much harder to game. That means you can push optimization a lot further without everything falling apart. It's a cleaner objective, and cleaner objectives let you scale.

Third, there's the shift in how we spend compute. We'd mostly thought of compute as something you spend in training. These approaches made it clear you can let the model think longer at inference time, with longer chains of thought, exploration and self-correction, and RL is what teaches the model to use that extra thinking productively rather than just rambling. Once you see that test-time compute is another axis you can scale along, the whole picture changes.

And honestly, part of it is that the recipe turned out to be simpler than many expected. There was a sense that you'd need elaborate search procedures, process reward models grading every step, and so on. What surprised a lot of people is how far you can get with fairly straightforward policy-gradient-style RL on outcome rewards, given a strong enough model and enough well-chosen problems. That simplicity is part of why it spread so quickly once people saw it working.

So I'd frame it less as "RL suddenly started working" and more as "the ingredients finally lined up": capable base models, robust rewards, enough compute and a willingness to let models think. The open question I find most exciting is how far this extends beyond domains with crisp verifiers, into areas where correctness is fuzzier. That's where much of the interesting work is now.

r002.rationale: It says the base models had to become capable enough to sometimes reason correctly before RL rewards became informative, making success appear overnight; it also says the approach spread quickly once people saw it working.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think "sudden" is the interesting word there, because from the inside it didn't feel sudden at all. It felt like a lot of ingredients had been sitting on the shelf for a while, and the thing that changed was mostly that the base models got good enough for them to combine.

So if you go back, RL on language models isn't new. People were doing RLHF, people were doing RL with code execution rewards, there were papers on math with verifiers years ago. What was missing, I think, was two things. One is that the pretrained model has to have a reasonable prior over good reasoning trajectories. If you're sampling and essentially never hit a correct chain, you have no signal, and RL just thrashes. Once the base models crossed some threshold where, on a hard math problem, maybe one in a hundred or one in a thousand samples was actually right, suddenly you have a gradient. And that threshold got crossed fairly quietly as a side effect of scaling and better pretraining data, not because anyone targeted it.

The second thing is a kind of change in belief about what the model was allowed to do. For a long time the implicit framing was: the answer should come out in a fixed budget, and chain of thought was this somewhat embarrassing trick. Letting the model spend a lot of tokens, letting it backtrack, letting it be wrong in the middle and then say "wait, actually," that was treated as noise to be cleaned up. And the realization, which I think o1 made undeniable, was that those behaviours are the capability. If you give the model a verifiable reward and enough freedom in the trajectory, it rediscovers things like checking its work and trying a second approach, because those are genuinely useful for getting the reward. You don't have to hand-design them.

And then the verifiable part matters a lot more than I would have guessed. The reward model story in RLHF was always a bit fragile, because the model learns to exploit the judge. With a ground-truth check, a unit test, a final numerical answer, you just don't have that failure mode in the same way. The model can't talk its way into a reward. So you can push much harder with optimization before things go off the rails, and that's a big part of why the gains look so steep.

I'd add one caveat, which is that I think people over-index on math and code because those are where it's easy to measure. The real question for me is how much of that reasoning transfers to domains where you don't have a verifier, and the honest answer right now is "some, but we don't fully understand how much or why." So I'd say the success is real, it's not magic, and the dynamics that made it work are fairly legible once you look at them. But I'd be careful about assuming the curve continues the same way once you leave the land of clean rewards.

astra-6.text:
I think the suddenness is partly about when we found the right setup, rather than reinforcement learning suddenly becoming a different technology. With something like mathematics or coding, you can let the model produce a fairly long solution and then check whether it got the answer right. That gives you a much cleaner training signal than trying to judge whether every individual step looks sensible.

But that only works if the model can already occasionally solve the problem. If every attempt fails, the reward doesn’t tell you much about what to do differently. So pretraining gives you this very capable starting point, with a lot of the ingredients for reasoning already there, and reinforcement learning can increase the probability of successful ways of using those ingredients.

The other important thing is that you’re giving the model room to compute before it answers. It can try an approach, notice a mistake, backtrack, check something. You don’t necessarily have to prescribe all those behaviors individually. If they help it reach a correct answer, an outcome reward can reinforce them.

So I’d understand it as a combination of sufficiently capable base models, reliable rewards, and enough room to explore solutions. Once those come together, something that previously looked quite brittle can start working remarkably well. And verifiable tasks are a particularly favorable place to see that happen; getting equally reliable learning signals for more open-ended work is a harder problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the surprising thing is less that reinforcement learning works and more that we’ve now got models that are good enough for it to work really well. If you give a model a difficult maths problem and it essentially never gets the answer right, a reward for correctness doesn’t give you much to learn from. But once pretraining gets you to the point where the model sometimes finds a solution, you can reinforce those successful attempts and build from there.

And verifiable rewards are particularly useful because you can let the model explore different ways of solving a problem without having to specify what every intermediate step should look like. You don’t need a human to judge whether a long argument sounds convincing; you can check whether the answer is correct, or whether the code passes the tests. That gives you a relatively reliable signal that you can scale.

So I’d understand it as a combination of a capability threshold from pretraining, a very useful source of reward, and enough compute to exploit it. It looks sudden because those ingredients come together and you start getting a strong improvement curve. But the underlying idea—that you can learn to solve problems by trying things and reinforcing what works—is very natural. The interesting question is how far that carries over into domains where checking an answer is much harder.
